paragraphs.text: Come, then: let us take up our subject, and you take up your listening. Let us all give ourselves to this evening's continuation of the story of Job, and with faith let us present ourselves to the word about endurance. For it would be absurd if Job, sitting on a dunghill, did not grow slack in his piety, while we, dancing in church, grow lazy toward the truth; or if he, surrounded by countless lamentations over his own misfortune, was not broken in soul, while we, surrounded by the singing of hymns and spiritual songs and the divine Scriptures, give up our eagerness to sloth. Job, his body eaten by worms, kept his soul unwounded in its piety. Worms did not defeat him; will sweat throw us in the wrestling match? Let us too become men, men according to the definition already given. For what marks a man is being blameless, righteous, true and God-fearing. In ordinary usage, when someone sends his servant or his son on some task, he urges him, saying, "Set about this task like a man," and so makes the common name a particular mark of admiration. In the same way, although all are called men, only he is truly a man who preserves the image and does not destroy the original beauty. Scripture called him a man so that, starting from our common nature, you might praise his purpose. It said he was from the land of Ausitis, so that you might sing the praises of the fruit that came from a land overgrown with impiety. It listed his possessions so that you might marvel at his advantages. It described his wealth, not so that you might praise his abundance, but so that you might marvel at him once he had been stripped bare. For he was stripped of everything, yet he was not stripped of his piety. He was like a city under siege, stripped of everything outside it and guarded by its wall alone. He was stripped of his children, yet he did not lose the fruits of piety. For he had the ways of piety as his children; he had the virtues as his daughters. He had three daughters according to the flesh and three virtues according to the spirit, as Paul says: "These three remain: faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love." He was stripped of everything, yet he did not deny the Creator of nature. For he knew that children are the comfort of succession, but God is the one who tends the root. He was not vexed to see the fruits cast off, for he knew that the one who tends the root remains forever. He was stripped of his sheep, yet he himself was a sheep guarded by God. He was stripped of his oxen: the yokes of oxen were taken from him, but the yoke of soul and body was not cut apart. Flesh and soul, in harmony together, drew the plough of piety. He received the fruits of virtue by way of endurance, so that he might multiply the fruits of endurance. So he had three thousand camels and five hundred grazing donkeys. In my view, what he possessed was little. For if he provided for every poor person, as he himself says, "I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame," then his property was small compared with his purpose, and what he spent on hospitality was greater than the abundance of his income. Job was poor, for he could not satisfy his eagerness to give. He was rich in possessions, but poor compared with the strength of his resolve. "And he had," it says, "great works on the earth." What were these? Love of the poor and hospitality, utmost humility, unsurpassed almsgiving, and everything that contributes to virtue. So he flourished in this way, not so much with passing wealth as with the wealth of piety. Another wise man, taking the word in its ordinary sense, thinks the great works were vineyards and olive groves and acres of sown land and the like. But in truth he had great works on the earth, flourishing as he was with heavenly wealth. Now the devil, as I said earlier in the previous sermon, the all-defiled one, suspected that just as virtue had grown rich along with Job while he was rich, so it would grow poor along with him once he became poor. So he strips him of his possessions in order to strip him also of the advantages of virtue, and he asks God for the trial against the righteous man. This is written so that you may take courage: a demon has no authority over a Christian, or over a man who fears God, unless permission is given from above, either for discipline or by God's allowance. For when God brings corrections, he either exacts a penalty for sins or trains virtue in divine achievements. So the devil could not make war on Job until God permitted him. And do not be surprised, beloved, that he had no authority over Job without receiving permission. He has no authority even over pigs. Hear how Legion pleaded: "If you cast us out, permit us to go into the pigs." If he has no authority over pigs without permission, how can he have authority over those made in the image of God without being ordered? "It happened," it says, "as on this day, that the angels of God came to stand before the Lord, and the devil stood in their midst." Does the devil, then, stand there together with the angelic service, and does the unclean spirit stand among the holy spirits? No: neither did the holy angels stand before God bodily, nor did Satan; rather, every kind of service is called "standing before." Elijah, while living on earth, was said to stand before God, as he says: "As the Lord lives, before whom I have stood this day." This does not mean he had gone up to heaven and stood there, but that he was serving the divine command. So too the devil stood, not in the heavenly realm or among the powers above the world, but as a creature of God he is ordered to do what is appointed. Hear how. Do not snatch at my words and say, "Does God use the devil as a servant?" Among human authorities there are soldiers in plain view who serve for marks of honor, and there are recognized soldiers set apart for punishments. So here too, holy angels are sent for good ministries and for God's dispensations on behalf of human beings, while demons are sent to punish lawless people. Hear how. When Paul mentions the holy angels, he says: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" From this it is clear that the holy angels serve the salvation of human beings, while the bitter demons serve the punishment of sinners. "For he sent out upon Egypt," says David, "wrath and anger and affliction, a mission by evil angels."

So the wicked and unclean demons, even though they have rebelled in their will, still lie under the yoke of servitude, and like executioners they are ordered to carry out what is commanded. And do not be surprised that God gives orders to demons. The apostles used the devil as an executioner. Paul says: "Since some have gone astray concerning the faith, I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may be taught not to blaspheme." And again, about someone who had committed fornication and deserved punishment, what does the same Paul say? "When you are assembled, and my spirit with you, with the power of the Lord Jesus, I have judged the man who has done this: he is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord." So that the demons may not think they have entirely seized power against God's authority, they are ordered, even against their will, to do what is commanded. These are not things that lead to prosperity but things that bring punishment. Have you not seen how our own magistrates act? When they summon someone with honor, they send the runners, called cursores in Latin; but when they drag people off in disgrace, they send out other soldiers, harsh and hard. In the same way God sends angels to the saints as ministers of salvation, but when he wishes to punish, he gives the demons leave. That is why, when God pronounced judgment against Ahab, he says: "Who will go and deceive Ahab, so that he will fall?" And an evil spirit answered: "Here I am." For it knew that the devil is appointed for this. So the demons — but forgive me, I beg you. I am speaking about things that are invisible and beyond the senses. I would never have attempted to say anything about such matters in the first place unless I had borrowed my starting points from holy Scripture. It is not within human understanding to distinguish the invisible from the visible; but since what God has said cannot be contradicted, we keep in step with what is written, whether we wish to or not. — So the most wicked demons are sent specifically to exact punishment from the wicked, but they are also sent to the righteous, not to punish them but to test them. Since a holy angel is not ordered to serve in testing, because God does not command an angel to do anything unworthy, the demons are permitted to carry out this testing. And do not be surprised that demons are sent to the righteous. The Master of all was once led up from the Jordan into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. If, then, the devil tempted the Lord and Savior of all, why should you be surprised if a demon is sent against a righteous man to train his endurance? He is sent, however, not by God's command but by his permission. Scripture shapes the account as though personifying the characters. For no voice comes from God to a wicked demon, nor is that transgressing will counted worthy of it. Its nature is good, but its will is evil, and it is not counted worthy of the pure voice. If you say, "The Lord said to the devil," I will answer you from David: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my statutes?" Did he utter a voice to the sinner? No. Rather, he speaks to the unworthy through the very things by which he expresses himself, through events themselves. God gave an order to the sea monster. Did he do so by sending out a voice or by giving force to some command? God gave an order to a worm at dawn. So if the account presents God as speaking to the devil, do not treat this disgraced and transgressing will as though it were on equal footing and brought into the Master's presence. The angels stood in their appointed order, but the devil came and stood among the angels, so that you may learn that he received the nature of an angel but displayed the will of a traitor. For "devil," brothers, is not the name of a nature but of a choice. Why "devil"? He was not a devil from the beginning; he was created an angel. He was named devil [diabolos] because he slanders [diaballōn] God to human beings and human beings to God, and because he sets master against servant and servant against master. When the devil suggests to us, "How many evils there are in the world! Where is God? Why does he not take charge?" he is slandering the Creator to us, for this has been the devil's work from the beginning. He slanders God to Adam, saying: "God knew that on the day you eat from the tree you will be like gods." God forbade you to eat, he says, out of envy. There he slanders God to Adam; here he slanders Job to God: "Does Job worship God for nothing?" That is: he is a hireling, not a virtuous man; he pays you a wage for his prosperity; take away his wealth and his real intention will be laid bare. So when God saw the righteous man insulted by the devil's suspicion, he takes away his possessions, in order to take away the suspicion and show his piety bare. And see the attitude of the wicked demon. "The Lord said to the devil," it says, "Where have you come from?" Then the proud and boastful one, knowing neither his own rank nor the dignity of the one questioning him, says: "I have gone around the earth and walked about under heaven, and here I am." He is all but shouting, wanting to show that he rules everything under heaven, that he has trodden all earthly things underfoot, that he has all human beings beneath his feet. "I have gone around the earth," he said, "and walked about under heaven, and here I am." The devil's boasting is cut down. Because he thought he ruled the image of God, he is cast out of the earth so that he may walk about there no longer, and the Master of all banishes him. For it is he who promised: "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God."

At first the devil walked about. When idolatry had spread everywhere, when impiety prevailed, when every kind of wickedness flourished, the devil walked about. But when there is holiness and righteousness and truth among those who keep the truth, God dwells and walks among them. "Have you set your mind," he says, "on my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth, blameless, righteous, true, keeping away from every evil?" The devil had said, "I have gone around everything under heaven," and was boasting as though he ruled all things. So the Word of truth, undoing his boast, says to him: "Have you seen the man you have not trodden underfoot, though you rule everything, as you said? Have you seen the man who has mastered all your wickedness? Have you seen the man who has trodden on you, who tread on everyone? Have you seen the man who has broken your tyranny, who has broken injustice by righteousness and impiety by piety?" But the devil sets himself against God and says: "He does not worship for nothing." He brought up the possessions in order to insult Job's way of life and his character, and to make his virtue look counterfeit through suspicion. "You have given him abundance," he says. "Take away the abundance, and his hypocrisy is exposed." God says to him: "Touch everything he has." For God knew that the devil's will was insatiably greedy, and he says: "See, I give you authority over everything; only do not touch him." He sets boundaries around the devil's wickedness. Now see what a bow he draws against the righteous man, what arrows he shoots. He went out, and first the worker of evils puts on a disguise, presenting himself as the messenger of the evils. He himself struck the livestock, and he himself reports the blow. "For the devil said to Job," it says, "Your yokes of oxen were ploughing and the female donkeys were grazing, and raiders came and slaughtered your servants, and I alone escaped and came to tell you." This is the devil's first trial, the first arrow against the noble contender. But Job raised against it the shield of faith, which can quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one. The yokes of oxen perished, but his soul was not divided. The donkeys perished, but the noble colt did not refuse the bridle of piety. He received the bitter news that his possessions were lost, and he stood firm like a secure and unconquerable tower. The devil, bitter in his wickedness and bitter in his purpose, regretted having reported it this way. Pay close attention, I beg you, so that the evil one's thinking does not escape you. The apostle too observed it closely, and says: "For we are not ignorant of his designs." He had reported to Job that the yokes of oxen were ploughing and the female donkeys were grazing and the raiders came. Then he saw Job bearing the news with a noble soul, and he regretted reporting it badly. The devil all but said to himself: "I reported it badly when I told him that men had made war on him. He can reason: 'If men made war on me and wronged me, what does that have to do with God?' I shot badly, I did not hit the mark, my shot failed, my arrows went astray. I said that men had carried off his goods. He can say: 'Why should I blame God for the injustice of men? Shall some be the wrongdoers and another be the one blasphemed?'" So, to shift Job's thoughts from human beings to God, and to show him that it was not men doing him harm but God making war on him, he says to him: "Fire fell from heaven." Can you say that enemies threw it down from above? Then insult the one who wronged you, blaspheme the one who made war on you! Fire fell from heaven. Why do you serve the one who wronged you? Why do you worship the one who is consuming your possessions? Fire fell from heaven. Job heard, and again he bore it nobly. For his endurance was truly endurance, sustained to the end, of which the Savior says: "The one who endures to the end will be saved." Fire fell from heaven. Every day he toiled to offer sacrifices for his children; what he toiled to offer day by day, God took all at once as a sacrifice. Fire fell from heaven. "If I alone were being clothed, I would rightly grieve. But if the poor were being clothed, can the Master neglect the poor? I know that what he took as a sacrifice he repays fivefold. Were my possessions gathered unjustly? Did I acquire my sheep through greed? The shoulders of the poor were warmed by the fleece of my sheep, and the mouth of the widow blessed me. God knows what he is doing. Now he has taken my property as a sacrifice, but he multiplies my wealth into an abundance of virtue. The arrows from outside do not shake me, for I am fortified within; rather, God's arrows strengthen me from within." For "the arrows of the Mighty One are sharpened"; of these David said, "Your arrows have pierced me." Which arrows? The arrow of piety, the arrow of righteousness, the arrow of longing for God, the arrow of zeal for virtue. It is by these divine arrows that the soul is wounded. So the devil had applied every trial and stripped Job of his possessions, yet he had not stripped him of virtue. Next he moves on to nature itself. He does violence to what nature had cultivated, tears the branches from the root, and crushes the children of the noble contender. He takes away the fruit in order to grieve the one who produced it. And what does he do? See the evil one's message too: how full of cunning it is, how close to sorcery, and how able to break the noble man's soul. He says to him: "While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking in the house of your eldest son, a great wind came from the desert and shook the house, and it fell on your little ones, and they died." The word is a diminutive, chosen to stir up grief. He did not say "on your children" but "on your little ones," so that hearing of the little ones Job might be moved to pity and bent toward grief. A great wind came from the desert. Again he slanders the Judge, for the wind obeys not human beings but God. It fell on your little ones, and they died. Then Job arose; for so it is written. "Arose" is well said. He did not collapse under the blow; he arose by the power of piety. He arose and worshipped. Worship was what he paid back for his misfortunes. Struck, he blessed; pelted with misfortunes, he gave thanks. And he cut off the hair of his head. Nowadays many of us who mourn let our hair grow, but he cut his off. Why? The mourner's aim is to change his condition into the opposite appearance. So where long hair is held in honor, leaving it uncut is a sign of mourning. Everywhere, mourners look for the opposite appearance. And he tore his garments. In appearance he was dragged down into grief, but in reality he was stripping for the contest of virtue. He strips off his garment so that, like a naked athlete, he may grapple with his opponent and, in a bout beyond dispute, win the prize for righteousness. He who was clothed with righteousness stripped off his garment, and the great lamp of piety says: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened; may the name of the Lord be blessed forever." O noble soul! These words became an arrow against the devil; these words shot arrows against the demons and broke the battle line of the enemy. "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall depart." These are apostolic words, showing manly courage before the age of the apostles. "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall depart" — just as the apostle says: "We brought nothing into the world; it is clear that we cannot take anything out either." The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.

To be brief, he was stripped of everything, and only his wife was left: the devil's old instrument. His wife was left, not because the devil spared her, but because he was keeping the weapon for himself. Since he knew that he had overthrown the first man through a woman, he holds the woman in reserve so that he can use the same weapon in his scheme. But there he found Adam, while here he does not find Adam. There he found Adam and Eve; here he found Eve, but he did not find Adam. His wife says to him: “How long will you hold out?” Truly these are the devil's words. For “how long” was the cry of the one being tormented. I am the one tormented, and you say, “How long?” I am the one being beaten, and are you the one who grows weary at the blows of the one tormented? “How long will you sit waiting, day after day, for deliverance?” Against his will the devil sings the praises of the righteous man's virtue and proclaims his endurance, showing that he struggled on in hope. “How long?” Then notice the wisdom of the writer. “And Job looked at her,” he says, “and spoke.” He did not say “paying attention to her,” but “looking at her.” “Looking at her”: why? Did he not know his own wife? Had he not lived with her? Had he not had children by her? Why, then, did he look at her? “Looking at her” shows that he does not see her, but the one inside her. Job looked at the devil; he saw the one who had spoken in the serpent and was now speaking in the woman, and he says: “You have spoken like one of the foolish women.” Why did he not say, “like one of the impious women, like one of the godless women”? He knew that she was not godless, but had been carried away by folly. Besides, brothers, the word “fool” is properly given to the one who denies God. For it says, “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” “Like one of the foolish women”: as if someone were saying, “You have spoken like Eve.” “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the bad?” O noble soul! Test his soul here, I beg you. Job did not know that he was contending for virtue; he did not know that he would be crowned for his endurance. He simply thought that it was a calamity sent by God. He thought these things were evils, and though he thought them evils, he did not blaspheme as one would over evils. If he fought like this while thinking them evils, would he not have fought far harder had he known about the crown? But why did God not tell him beforehand: “See what you are doing! The devil is about to draw up his ranks against you, he is about to arm himself against you. Fight, be strong, so that he does not turn your mind aside, so that he does not plunder your thoughts, so that he does not lay siege to your soul. Be strong”? And do not think it unfitting for God to forewarn the athlete about the bout. For the Lord says to Peter: “Peter, look, Satan has demanded to have you, to sift you like wheat.” He foretells their trials to the apostles, yet to Job he foretells neither the trials nor the contest. Is there injustice with God? By no means! Some he encourages, others he leaves alone. Why does he not speak to him as he did to the apostles? God knew the devil's malice; he knew his envy; he knew the suspicion that could blunt virtue. Suppose God had said to him: “Watch yourself, and fight. If you endure to the end, I will give you back your possessions twice over; you will inherit the kingdom of heaven; you will receive crowns of immortality; the whole world will be full of your praises and commendations.” Had he said this, the righteous man would indeed have fought, but the devil would again have found a pretext. If Job had won after fighting on those terms, the devil would have said to God: “Did he fight for nothing? You promised him immortality, you promised him a kingdom, you promised him crowns.” So if, when he enjoyed temporal goods, he was suspected of being not a righteous man but a hireling, would the devil not have found a far greater pretext if he had received the promise of eternal goods? Instead God hides the crowns in order to lay bare the contests; he hides the prize in order to reveal the athlete. Then why, someone asks, did he not hide it from the apostles too? If this is why he did not tell Job, why did he not keep silent about the prize in the same way with the apostles? Job was fighting alone; he toiled for himself, he fought for himself. The apostles, however, were heralds to the earth and teachers of the whole world. He could have hidden it from them, but the world would have suffered loss from it. Paul could have fought without a promise of crowns, Peter could have shown courage without a promise, the apostles could have fought for virtue without receiving any promise of good things. But Paul is not everywhere, Peter is not everywhere; the souls of many are weak, the minds of many give way. For if today, when the kingdom is preached, and the enjoyment of good things to come, and life in the company of angels, and the delights of paradise, many still despise what has been promised because they cling to present things, then if it had been kept entirely silent, who would have run to piety? Rightly, then, brothers, he does not show Job the things to come, in order to display the firmness of his resolve, while to the apostles he promises the things to come, in order to rouse the souls of their hearers and to put strength into the mind of the world. Many now hear about the kingdom and despise it; many await Christ and put on wickedness; many do not withdraw from vice. Many today honor the fasts and say: “Today I will say nothing to my opponent. Let the day of Christ's passion pass, and I will press my lawsuit, avenge the insult, and do plenty.” Then you are a brother of Esau if you think such things; you are saying the same things Esau said. For Esau too wanted to kill his brother, but he respected his father. And what did he say? “Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, and then I will kill my brother Jacob.” Let my father's death pass, and then I will do away with him. And what do you say? Let the passion of Christ pass, and then I will march against my enemy. Watch out that you are not a brother of Esau. Hear what Paul says: “Let no one be a fornicator or profane like Esau, so that many are not defiled through him.” I have said these things not to provoke you, but for the help and salvation of the brothers. May it be granted to us, taught by the word and guided by the histories, and setting ourselves right by the contests of the holy fathers and prophets, always to send up glory to God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
